query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a precisely controlled heat treatment profile — specifically, tailored annealing temperatures and cooling rates monitored in situ by X‐ray diffraction (XRD) — will steer phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys towards the formation and stabilization of desired microstructures.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-solidified Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA exhibiting a multiphase microstructure with unpredictable phase distributions.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal processing using a heat treatment profile that precisely sets the annealing temperature and cooling rate, combined with in situ XRD monitoring.
generation.conditions: Thermal processing performed under inert or vacuum environments with a range of annealing temperatures and defined quenching rates to capture real-time phase transformation kinetics.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of phase boundaries and local chemical order during thermal treatment, as detected by in situ XRD.
generation.mechanism: The controlled thermal energy input and rapid cooling modify atomic diffusion kinetics, promoting selective nucleation and growth of targeted phases while suppressing undesired transformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: A more predictable and stabilized microstructure characterized by the preferential formation of desired constituent phases, which should translate into improved mechanical properties compared to conventionally treated alloys.
generation.baseline: Heat treatments with non-optimized annealing and cooling parameters that result in unpredictable phase mixtures and suboptimal material properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys processed under similar compositional and thermal conditions; variations in alloy composition or significant changes in processing environment may yield different phase evolution kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal ranges for annealing temperature and cooling rates remain uncertain and may require further iterative refinement via experimental feedback.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA and subject each to different heat treatment profiles varying in annealing temperature and cooling rate while using in situ XRD to record phase evolution in real time. After processing, perform complementary microstructural analyses using scanning and transmission electron microscopy to quantify phase compositions.
measurements: In situ XRD patterns to track phase transformation kinetics
SEM/TEM imaging for microstructure and phase distribution analysis
Mechanical property tests for correlating microstructural changes with performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant correlation is observed between the controlled heat treatment parameters and the evolution or stabilization of targeted phases (i.e., phase distributions remain inconsistent regardless of the processing profile), or if the microstructure does not exhibit the predicted phase transformations, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. decision.trend: Early studies on Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs demonstrated that the processing route (e.g., arc-melting, irradiation) heavily influences the precipitation and phase stability, as seen in the 2016 work where different Al contents led to varying irradiation-induced precipitation behaviors. Later, high-pressure and high-temperature treatments (PMC11087546) were used to produce hierarchically patterned microstructures that improved both strength and ductility, underscoring how external processing conditions can modify phase evolution. Most recently, aging experiments on eutectic variants (PMC12806431) reveal that carefully controlled isothermal treatments can drive transitions (e.g., tempering-like embrittlement versus ductility recovery) by altering precipitate size and ordering. This trend shows a progressive move from passive observation of phase formation toward active manipulation of the microstructure via thermal processing.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, a predictive understanding and fine control of the phase transformation pathways during thermal processing in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs remains unsolved. In particular, it is challenging to tune the annealing and quenching parameters to select desired phases without triggering undesired transformations that degrade properties.
decision.lever: heat treatment profile (annealing temperature and cooling rate) via controlled annealing and quenching experiments combined with in-situ XRD analysis
decision.why: Building on the established sensitivity of phase evolution to thermal treatment conditions, the most plausible next step is to refine the processing window by leveraging advanced in-situ measurements. This approach will allow researchers to directly correlate specific annealing and cooling parameters with phase transformation kinetics in real time, thereby enabling a more predictable control of constituent phase formation and stabilization in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
